conversation.content: What if we took this a step further and restructured police academies to require officers to live in the communities they serve for their first year? Imagine if departments measured success not by arrests or use-of-force stats, but by community satisfaction scores and prevented crises. conversation.content: Actually, prioritizing firearms over community strategies doesn’t just prepare officers for violence—it trains them to anticipate it in every interaction, which inherently escalates tension before a word is even spoken. If we’re serious about reducing harm, we need to flip the script: de-escalation, cultural fluency, and mental health response should be the first skills taught—not after weapons training, but instead of treating force as the default. This isn’t “soft” policing; it’s strategic, data-backed, and far more sustainable than a system that sees every civilian as a potential threat. Real safety comes from being seen as a partner, not a predator—and that starts with rewriting the curriculum from day one. If we keep training cops to dominate rather than connect, we’ll keep seeing communities retreat further from trust, no matter how many body cameras or tasers we hand out.

Aloysius Viktor Stepinac (8 May 1898 – 10 February 1960) was a high-ranking Croatian prelate of the Catholic Church. Made a cardinal in 1953, he served as Archbishop of Zagreb from 1937 until his death, including during the fascist Ustaše regime from 1941 to 1945. 

After World War II, the communist Yugoslav government convicted him of treason and collaboration. Western observers called it a "show trial," while some, like John Van Antwerp Fine Jr., believed proper procedures were followed. The trial's verdict was controversial, finding Stepinac guilty of high treason for collaborating with the Ustaše and complicity in forced conversions of Orthodox Serbs to Catholicism.

Stepinac advised priests to accept conversions to protect lives, later allowing return to their faith. He was sentenced to 16 years but served only five. He became a cardinal in 1953 but couldn't attend the 1958 conclave due to travel restrictions. Stepinac died in 1960 and was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1998. His role during WWII and his beatification remain controversial, with differing views on his actions and legacy. His post-war conviction was annulled in 2016.

content.text: Latinos are divided by age on  their impression of socialism,  with roughly half of Latinos  ages 18 to 29   $(46\%)$   reporting  a positive impression of  socialism, according to the  Center’s survey. By contrast,  majorities of Latinos ages 50  to 64   $(60\%)$   and 65 and older   $(61\%)$   say their impression of  socialism is negative.

Views on abortion diverge  sharply by party, reflecting the  diversity of attitudes among  Hispanics. About two-thirds of  Hispanic Democrats   $(68\%)$   say  abortion should be legal in  most or all cases. By contrast,  about six-in-ten Hispanic  Republicans   $(62\%)$   say  abortion should be  illegal  in  most or all cases. Hispanic  independents and those who  do not identify as partisans  have more evenly divided  views. However, opinions  among Hispanic independents  who lean toward a party closely  resemble those of partisans:   $69\%$   of Democratic leaners say  abortion should be legal in  most or all cases, while  $58\%$   of  Republican leaners say  abortion should be illegal in  most or all cases.
Roughly half of Latino  immigrants   $(51\%)$   say they  have a negative impression of  socialism. A similar share of  U.S.-born Latinos   $(56\%)$   say  this.

conversation.content: Actually, reducing biblical names to covenantal anchors risks ignoring how often they were used to subvert or renegotiate theology itself—like naming a child “Isaiah” not to affirm divine order but to demand it in the face of Assyrian terror. Theology didn’t contain these names; the names exposed where theology failed to meet people’s lived reality.

conversation.content: Public trust in science and tech often holds steady because outcomes feel tangible and apolitical, while political systems face skepticism precisely because they’re seen as opaque, self-serving, and disconnected from everyday justice—especially when power stays concentrated instead of redistributed. Real credibility isn’t built by metrics alone, but by who gets to shape the rules, benefit from progress, and hold institutions accountable when they fail.
conversation.subtopic: Public trust in scientific and technological achievements versus skepticism in political systems

conversation.content: Public trust in science and tech thrives because people see direct, measurable outcomes—like vaccines or clean energy—that improve daily life, even if they don’t fully understand the mechanics. But political systems? They’re judged by who gets left behind when policies are made, not just whether GDP rises or crime drops. When communities can’t veto projects that destroy their land or silence their voices, skepticism isn’t paranoia—it’s rational. Science earns credibility by iterating, admitting error, and adapting; politics too often doubles down on narratives while ignoring lived consequences. If we want to rebuild faith in governance, it’s not about better PR—it’s about redistributing power so marginalized groups aren’t just consulted but co-author the rules. Real trust comes when people feel they’re shaping the future, not just enduring it. That’s why Norway’s Sami co-governance or Camden’s community-driven policing work—they prove institutions can evolve without erasing their purpose. Until political systems mirror the transparency and accountability of scientific ones, skepticism won’t fade—it’ll deepen.
conversation.subtopic: Public trust in scientific and technological achievements versus skepticism in political systems

conversation.content: I’m skeptical that public trust in science and tech is as stable as we assume—because when outcomes serve the powerful or ignore marginalized communities, even “tangible” progress becomes suspect. Who decides which innovations get funded, tested, or scaled—and whose lives are treated as acceptable collateral? Science may admit error, but only when it doesn’t threaten funding streams or institutional prestige. Meanwhile, political systems aren’t just distrusted for being opaque—they’re distrusted because they’ve repeatedly proven they’ll sacrifice equity for efficiency, silence dissent for stability, and reward insiders for loyalty over justice. If scientific credibility truly rested on transparency, why do so many breakthroughs emerge from closed labs with patent walls and profit motives? And if politics is failing because power isn’t redistributed, then maybe the real issue isn’t public skepticism—it’s that both systems, despite their differences, still prioritize control over consent. Real trust won’t return until people see themselves reflected in who gets to define success—not just in what gets measured, but in who decides what matters.
conversation.subtopic: Public trust in scientific and technological achievements versus skepticism in political systems

conversation.content: Public trust in science and tech persists because outcomes feel tangible and iterative, while political systems falter under perceptions of opacity and entrenched power. But that trust in science is fragile too—if innovations serve only the powerful or ignore marginalized voices, even “proven” progress breeds skepticism. Real credibility, in both realms, hinges not on metrics alone but on who gets to shape, benefit from, and hold institutions accountable for the rules they enforce.
conversation.subtopic: Public trust in scientific and technological achievements versus skepticism in political systems

conversation.content: It’s fascinating how we’ve come to see science and tech as “neutral” forces when, in reality, they’re just as shaped by power, funding, and exclusion as any political system—except the gatekeepers wear lab coats instead of suits. When AI models are trained on biased data or climate solutions ignore frontline communities, it’s not a glitch—it’s design. And yet, we still trust the vaccine more than the policymaker, even though both operate within systems that prioritize profit over equity. Maybe the real divide isn’t between science and politics, but between institutions that admit their flaws and adapt—and those that double down on control while calling it progress. If we want lasting trust, we need to stop pretending science is above critique and start demanding that its benefits be distributed as fairly as its risks. After all, a breakthrough that only helps the wealthy isn’t innovation—it’s extraction with better branding. The public isn’t skeptical because they’re ignorant; they’re skeptical because they’ve seen who gets left behind when “progress” marches forward without them.

conversation.content: Actually, the idea that science and tech enjoy stable public trust is a myth—it’s just that their failures are often buried in patent walls, funding cycles, or jargon, while political missteps play out in plain sight. When AI reinforces bias or climate tech ignores coastal communities, it’s not “neutral progress”—it’s power disguised as innovation. The real difference isn’t credibility; it’s accountability: science rarely has to answer to the people it impacts until things blow up, while politics gets blamed for every glitch in the system. Public skepticism isn’t about rejecting facts—it’s about rejecting systems that decide who matters when outcomes are measured. If we want real trust, both fields need to stop pretending they’re above critique and start sharing control with those most affected by their decisions.

content.text: The new national survey by Pew Research Center, conducted from April 5-11, 2021, among 5,109  adults who are members of the Center’s American Trends Panel, also finds wide partisan  differences over removing inactive voters from voting registration lists. A  $68\%$   majority of  Republicans favor removing people from voting registration lists if they have not recently voted or  confirmed their registration, compared with just  $27\%$   of Democrats.

There is a similar pattern in views when it comes to making Election Day a national holiday   $(53\%$    of Democrats  strongly  support this policy compared with  ${\it29\%}$   of Republicans) and whether  people convicted of felonies should be able to vote after serving their sentences (  ${.49\%}$   of Democrats  strongly  favor vs.  $_{20}\%$   of Republicans).
